cells.tense: The pen is in your hand now and the drawing is going somewhere.
cells.ask: Put in an hour at the table without checking what it's for, the way you show up for anything else that matters.
cells.core:
You sit down with something half-formed and you don't rush it into a shape it hasn't earned. The work gets your attention, not your panic. When it comes out strange, that's information rather than failure — you go back the next day and keep going.

That patience is a real skill, built by hours. So when you're wondering what to do next, the answer isn't a new plan. It's in the practice — showing up at the table again, even when it feels small and ordinary. The depth comes from repetition, not from a breakthrough. Staying with what isn't finished yet, letting it take the time it takes — that's what the hours have been teaching you.
cells.sheetLine: You can sit with not-knowing and let the work arrive on its own time.
cells.verb: moving through uncertainty without forcing it to resolve
cells.place: a table you return to on your own, where a small steady light gets kept lit by attention

cells.tense: You're somewhere ahead in a version of this that hasn't arrived, bracing for it.
cells.ask: Spend ten minutes at the table watching what's actually there before touching it — just looking, no fixing.
cells.core:
There's a finished version of this in your head and it's gotten very detailed. Compared to that, whatever's on the table right now looks like nothing, so you push it toward the shape you already see. The push is the problem. You're treating the materials as obstacles instead of as things that have their own timing.

What the vision needs is care, the slow kind that lets a thing grow instead of yanking it into place. Half-done isn't failure here; it's the stage you're in. The pressure to arrive fast is the thing keeping the work far away from you. Ease off it and the thing on the table gets room to become what it might be.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door you already walked through, waiting for permission.
cells.ask: Open the sketchbook to one page, put down a mark with your eyes closed, and close it without looking at what you made.
cells.core:
You know how to do this. The hand is steady, the eye is trained — years of practice stand behind you. But somewhere along the way the work stopped getting to have its own intelligence. Everything has to make sense now or it doesn't count. No wandering, no play.

The instinct hasn't left you. It's just not getting any air. A vision quest or a breakthrough isn't what's missing — the habit of checking whether it's allowed is what's holding the line shut. Put a mark down without knowing where it's going. Not to be good. Just to keep the line open.
cells.sheetLine: You know how to make the work. The distrust is what's holding it back.

cells.tense: You're already writing this and you haven't picked up the pen.
cells.ask: Count what you've actually made in the last month — pages, sketches, whatever holds it — and say the number out loud once.
cells.core:
The dreaming is running whether you claim it or not. You move through a day and the work is quietly shaping it — what you notice, what you collect, what keeps coming back. But if someone asked what you're doing, you'd probably say nothing. The making runs; the saying so doesn't.

The practice is what brings it into the open. Not to prove anything — to see it. Solitude at the table is where the dream gets a body. When you count what you've made, you're not taking a test. You're letting the work be what it is. The quiet line between you and the page is already there. Step onto it.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim I'd flag in my own draft: saying the person's night work is going well is fine, but any line implying the drawing is what makes it safe, or that sheer volume is why it lands, goes past what the record supports. The reader could reasonably say 'the practice is just how I hold a day together, it isn't going anywhere.' The asks all survive a wrong read — an hour at the table with the sketchbook, ten minutes of watching without fixing, one blind mark left in the book, a count of what actually got made are each useful with none of my claims being true. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'trust the process', which flatters the writer and hands the person nothing.
